title: 5mo M Severe Bronchiolitis
chiefComplaint: Working hard to breathe and not feeding
background: Five month old, born at 34 weeks, weight 5.8 kg. Four days of coryza then progressive cough and noisy breathing. Today he has taken less than a third of his normal feeds, has had two brief pauses in breathing that frightened his mother, and has had four wet nappies in 24 hours instead of the usual eight. His two year old sister has a cold. It is peak season, and the department has seen nineteen similar infants this week. Most of them needed nothing. This one does.

exam.finding: Miserable, exhausted rather than agitated, which is the more worrying of the two. Grunting intermittently. Too breathless to feed

Profuse clear nasal secretions blocking both nostrils (infants are obligate nasal breathers, so this alone worsens the work of breathing), head bobbing, nasal flaring, dry mucous membranes, anterior fontanelle slightly sunken
Tachycardia at 182/min, capillary refill 3 seconds, femoral pulses present and equal, no murmur, no hepatomegaly to suggest cardiac failure

Respiratory rate 72 with marked subcostal, intercostal and sternal recession, tracheal tug. Widespread fine inspiratory crackles with expiratory wheeze in all zones. Prolonged expiratory phase. Observed apnoeic pause of 12 seconds during examination
Soft, mildly distended from air swallowing, liver edge palpable 1 cm below the costal margin which is normal at this age and displaced by hyperinflation, no masses
Perioral cyanosis during coughing episodes, mottled peripheries, reduced turgor, capillary refill 3 seconds, no rash

GCS 14, drowsy and less responsive than his mother describes as normal, normal tone, anterior fontanelle sunken. Drowsiness in bronchiolitis means carbon dioxide retention and exhaustion, and it is the sign that predicts intubation

investigations.name: Pulse oximetry on room air
investigations.report: Persistent hypoxaemia. Saturation is the single most useful measurement in bronchiolitis and it is one of the few that should change your decision.

investigations.name: Capillary blood gas
investigations.report: Respiratory acidosis with carbon dioxide retention, confirming exhaustion. Do not perform this routinely in bronchiolitis. It is indicated here because of the apnoeas and the drowsiness.

investigations.name: Respiratory viral PCR (nasopharyngeal)
investigations.report: Positive. Does not change treatment for this infant, but it does determine cohorting and isolation, which is why it is worth doing in an admitted patient and not worth doing in one going home.

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.report: Hyperinflation with flattened hemidiaphragms, peribronchial thickening and patchy right middle lobe atelectasis. No lobar consolidation, no effusion. Routine chest X-ray in bronchiolitis increases antibiotic prescribing without improving outcomes, because atelectasis is repeatedly misread as pneumonia. It is justified here by the severity and the oxygen requirement.

investigations.name: Sodium
investigations.report: Mild hyponatraemia, common in bronchiolitis from inappropriate ADH secretion. Use isotonic fluid and restrict to two thirds maintenance.

investigations.name: White cell count and CRP
investigations.report: Unremarkable, consistent with a viral illness. Serious bacterial co-infection occurs in under 1% of infants with typical bronchiolitis.

data.label: Nasal suction and oxygen
actions: Oxygen to target saturations 92% or above

doseMap.Gentle nasal suction: Cheap, immediately effective, and repeatedly forgotten. Clearing the nose alone can drop the respiratory rate substantially in an obligate nasal breather
doseMap.Oxygen to target saturations 92% or abov: Do not chase 100%. Higher targets prolong admission without benefit

data.label: Escalate respiratory support for apnoea and exhaustion
actions: Prepare for CPAP if no improvement

doseMap.High flow nasal cannula oxygen: 2 L/kg/min (about 12 L/min for 5.8 kg), heated and humidified. Reassess at 60 to 90 minutes. Failure to improve by then predicts the need for CPAP or intubation

data.label: Hydration by the least invasive route that works
actions: Restrict to two thirds maintenance with isotonic fluid
Strict fluid balance and daily sodium

doseMap.Nasogastric feeding or IV fluids: Nasogastric feeding is preferred if the respiratory rate allows, since it preserves gut function and avoids a cannula. At 72 breaths per minute the aspiration risk is significant, so IV is the safer choice tonight
doseMap.Restrict to two thirds maintenance with: Roughly 39 mL/h at full maintenance for 5.8 kg, so about 26 mL/h. Fluid restriction reflects the SIADH risk

data.label: Withhold the treatments that do not work
actions: No antibiotics without evidence of bacterial infection

doseMap.No salbutamol: Multiple trials show no benefit in bronchiolitis under 12 months. A transient improvement in wheeze is not the same as a shorter admission or less oxygen. Prescribing it is the commonest error in this diagnosis

data.label: Response to high flow
data.narrative: After 90 minutes on high flow the respiratory rate falls to 54, recession lessens, saturations reach 94% and the apnoeas stop. Repeat gas shows a pCO2 of 52 and a pH of 7.32. He avoids intubation.

data.label: Explain why you are deliberately not prescribing anything, and mean it (Empathy)
data.narrative: His mother has been to two clinics and both gave salbutamol and an antibiotic, and she reasonably concludes that this hospital is doing less for a sicker child. You explain that oxygen, suction and feeding are the treatment, that the drugs she was given do not work for this illness, and that the reason he is now improving is the support and not a prescription. Then you show her the numbers on the monitor going the right way. Dr. Bob calls it a waste of eight minutes. She brings her daughter to this department instead of a clinic four months later, on day one instead of day four.

data.label: Admit with clear escalation criteria
actions: Discharge criteria: maintaining saturations in air and feeding above 75% of normal

data.label: Course
data.narrative: Peak severity at day 5 of illness, which is typical. Weaned off high flow on day 3 of admission and off oxygen on day 4. Feeding fully by day 5.

data.label: Disposition
data.narrative: Discharged day 5 with advice that the cough will continue for two to four weeks, which prevents three unnecessary return visits. Prematurity at 34 weeks is documented as a risk factor for next season. No antibiotics, no salbutamol and no steroids were given at any point.
